meta.title: Who really said "Fashion fades, only style remains the same"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not in these words. Quote Investigator documents Chanel's own 1965 wording as 'Mode passes; style remains' — the popular English line is a later paraphrase.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Fashion fades, only style remains the same'?
meta.ogDescription: Chanel expressed the idea in a 1965 McCall's interview — as 'Mode passes; style remains.' The exact popular wording isn't documented from her.

answer.label: Not Coco Chanel’s words — a later paraphrase
answer.authorDates: 1883–1971 · French couturière, founder of the House of Chanel
answer.sourceLine: Chanel really did draw this distinction — but not in this sentence. In a McCall’s interview published in November 1965 she said “Mode passes; style remains,” the wording Quote Investigator ↗ credits to her. The familiar line “Fashion fades, only style remains the same” is documented nowhere in her lifetime: Wikiquote ↗ can cite it only to a September 1994 issue of Architectural Digest, a magazine page printed long after her death in 1971.
answer.confidenceText: The thought is genuinely hers. This English sentence is not documented from her.

source.excerpt: That is real style. The rest is mode. Mode passes; style remains.
trail: 25 August 1929 — the Springfield Republican prints what Quote Investigator ↗ calls “an excellent example of the maxim under investigation using a different phrasing”: an unnamed “philosophical beauty expert” saying “Fashion comes and goes, style goes on forever.” Anything later, QI notes, is arguably derivative — though QI records the idea earlier still, in an 1889 book of sketches from Mexico and in a 1904 architectural review (“The fashions of architecture—they perish. Style endures.”). QI reserves the term “earliest close match” for Chanel’s 1965 McCall’s line, not for this one.
November 1965 — Chanel gives her own version in McCall’s, interviewed by Joseph Barry: “Mode passes; style remains.” QI ↗ verified the issue on paper (p. 170).
1966 — Barry reprints the interview, aphorism included, in his book The People of Paris (Doubleday, Garden City, N.Y.) ↗; a copy is held, access-restricted, at the Internet Archive ↗.

1994 onward — the wording “Fashion fades, only style remains the same” circulates on one lone secondary citation, Architectural Digest (September 1994), p. 30, carried by Wikiquote ↗ and copied by the aggregators.
source.excerptNote: From Chanel’s answer about being copied, in the McCall’s interview published November 1965, as quoted by Quote Investigator ↗, which verified the issue on paper. Note her word is mode, not fashion.

source.rightsNote: No rights status can honestly be asserted for this exact English sentence: no author, work or date of first publication has been documented for it, and the only citation offered is a 1994 magazine page. Separately, Chanel’s documented wording is not free to reuse either — it was first published in McCall’s in November 1965 and reprinted in Joseph Barry’s The People of Paris (Doubleday, 1966), both well after 1931 and so still in copyright.

author.name: Coco Chanel
author.heading: Coco Chanel
author.metaLine: 1883–1971 · French couturière, founder of the House of Chanel
author.bio: Gabrielle Bonheur “Coco” Chanel (1883–1971) built the House of Chanel and reshaped twentieth-century dress around simplicity, comfort and the individual wearer. She relaunched her couture house in 1954 and was still granting interviews in her eighties, which is when the fashion-versus-style distinction was actually taken down from her. She wrote no memoir, so almost everything she is quoted as saying reaches us through journalists — a gap that has made her one of the most freely paraphrased names in the language.

cite.sourceCitation: Chanel's documented wording: Joseph Barry, “An Interview with Chanel,” McCall's, November 1965, 170; reprinted in Joseph Barry, The People of Paris (Garden City, N.Y.: Doubleday & Company, 1966), 62. The popular English wording “Fashion fades, only style remains the same” is cited by Wikiquote only to Architectural Digest, September 1994, 30. Family of sayings traced in “Quote Origin: Fashion Passes; Style Remains,” Quote Investigator, March 15, 2013.

misattribution.heading: What the famous wording gets wrong
misattribution.intro: The sentence is printed under Coco Chanel’s name on quote sites, tote bags and shop windows. The idea behind it really is hers — the words are not documented anywhere in her lifetime.

items.why: Wikiquote ↗ lists the line with one citation only — “As quoted in Architectural Digest (September 1994), p. 30” — a magazine page from more than two decades after she died. Quote Investigator’s ↗ study of the saying does not record this English sentence from Chanel at all.

Interviewed by journalist Joseph Barry, she said: “That is real style. The rest is mode. Mode passes; style remains.” Quote Investigator ↗ verified the issue on paper and notes it is unclear whether she spoke the aphorism in French or English.

The one documented couturier wording that uses “fade” is Saint Laurent’s — “Fashions fade, style is eternal” — recorded in The Columbia Dictionary of Quotations, which cites Andy Warhol’s Interview of 13 April 1975, as reproduced by Quote Investigator ↗. That is an observation about the wording, not proof of where the popular sentence came from.

items.scope: Already circulating before either of them
items.why: The Springfield Republican of 25 August 1929 carries the maxim in what Quote Investigator ↗ calls “an excellent example of the maxim under investigation using a different phrasing,” credited to no one: an unnamed “philosophical beauty expert” saying “Fashion comes and goes, style goes on forever.” QI notes that remarks after this date are arguably derivative — and records the idea earlier still, in 1889 and in a 1904 architectural review. “Earliest close match” is QI’s label for Chanel’s 1965 line, not for this one.
Sites such as AZQuotes ↗ carry the line with the identical Architectural Digest, September 1994, page 30 reference — the same lone secondary citation, copied onward rather than independently checked.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest verdict, following Quote Investigator ↗: Chanel is fairly credited with a stylish expression of this idea — but the one she is documented giving, in November 1965, is “Mode passes; style remains.” The saying itself was already in print anonymously by 1929, and “Fashion fades, only style remains the same” is a later paraphrase with no traceable author.

context.heading: Why this one is so hard to pin down
lead: Two words doing very different jobs — that was Chanel’s actual point, and she made it plainly. Fashion is the thing you use up; style is the thing that survives being used. The sentence the internet prints under her photograph carries that idea faithfully. It simply is not the sentence she is documented saying.

What she is documented saying appeared in a McCall’s interview conducted by the journalist Joseph Barry, published in November 1965, when — as Quote Investigator ↗ notes — she was an eminent 81-year-old. Her word was mode, not fashion, and her verb was passes, not fades. The English line everyone quotes turns up later, and the earliest citation anyone offers for it is a magazine page from 1994.
detailsBody: The distinction long predates Chanel. Quote Investigator ↗ finds it applied to buildings in a 1904 review of domestic architecture (“Style endures”), and then, in a Springfield, Massachusetts newspaper of 25 August 1929, in the mouth of an unnamed “philosophical beauty expert” discussing the sun-tan fad.

It kept changing hands afterwards. In February 1969 Studs Terkel, writing to the editors of the New York Times Book Review, credited “Fashion passes; style remains” to the architect Pier Luigi Nervi; by 2012 a version was being credited to the fashion editor Diana Vreeland. All of this is laid out in QI’s chronology ↗.

Even the company paraphrased her. A Chanel Corporation advertisement of 5 December 1983 gave her credo as “Fashion passes, style remains” — which, as Quote Investigator ↗ points out, does not precisely match the words printed under her name in 1965.
context.pull: Her word was ‘mode,’ and her verb was ‘passes.’ The famous version changed both.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator documents Chanel's 1965 McCall's wording as "Mode passes; style remains," an anonymous 1929 Springfield Republican version "Fashion comes and goes, style goes on forever," a 1904 architectural variant "Style endures," Studs Terkel's 1969 credit to Pier Luigi Nervi, Yves Saint Laurent's "Fashions fade, style is eternal" (Columbia Dictionary of Quotations, citing Andy Warhol's Interview, 13 April 1975), and a December 1983 Chanel Corporation advertisement giving her credo as "Fashion passes, style remains" — and it does not document the wording "Fashion fades, only style remains the same."

Wikiquote's Coco Chanel page lists "Fashion fades, only style remains the same." with the single citation "As quoted in Architectural Digest (September 1994), p. 30," in an undifferentiated "Quotes" section with no Sourced/Attributed/Misattributed subheadings.
Wikiquote's Fashion page carries the same line credited to Coco Chanel with the same Architectural Digest (September), p. 30, 1994 citation.
AZQuotes reproduces "Fashion fades, only style remains the same." under Coco Chanel's name with the citation Architectural Digest magazine, page 30, September 1994.
Joseph (Amber) Barry's The People of Paris was published by Doubleday in Garden City, N.Y., in 1966.
The Internet Archive holds a copy of Joseph Barry's The People of Paris (1966); the item is access-restricted.
Gabrielle Bonheur "Coco" Chanel was born 19 August 1883 and died 10 January 1971; she was a French designer who founded the House of Chanel and relaunched her couture business in 1954.
